passages.text: Alzheimer’s disease: genetic background in the era of next-generation sequencing technologies
Abstract

While rare, highly penetrant variants in <italic toggle="yes">APP</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PSEN1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">PSEN2</italic> are associated with early-onset Alzheimer’s disease, especially its familial form, the disease in general is shaped by a complex interplay of various genetic factors. <sentence_start/>Both common and rare variants across numerous loci, which were identified mainly during large genome-wide association studies, contribute to disease risk, phenotypic heterogeneity and progression in both early- and late-onset forms. <sentence_start/>This review synthesizes current understanding of the genetic architecture of Alzheimer's disease in the era of next-generation sequencing, with particular emphasis on variant classes beyond single nucleotide polymorphisms. <sentence_start/>Structural variants, including copy number variations, tandem repeat expansions and transposable element insertions, are considered as potential contributors to the ‘missing heritability’ in Alzheimer's disease. <sentence_start/>In addition, we discuss somatic mosaicism that represents another layer of its complexity. <sentence_start/>We highlight how whole-genome sequencing, combined with advanced bioinformatic pipelines and reference resources, enables systematic detection of different variant types. <sentence_start/>We also outline the translational potential of genetic discoveries, including polygenic risk and hazard score models for patient stratification, and underscore the importance of integrative genomic and multi-omic approaches in advancing precision medicine in Alzheimer's disease.

Lukyova <italic toggle="yes">et al</italic>. provide an overview of the genetic background of Alzheimer’s disease in the era of next-generation sequencing. <sentence_start/>By integrating knowledge on both small and structural variants, somatic mosaicism and polygenic risk/hazard modelling, they highlight emerging mechanisms that may explain missing heritability and highlight AI-driven multi-omic integration for personalized disease prediction.

Introduction

Alzheimer's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disease characterized by a specific pattern of cognitive and functional decline that correlates with advancing age and is associated with distinct neuropathological changes.<citation rid="fcag332-B1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21371747" doi="10.1016/S0140-6736(10)61349-9" count="1"><sup>1</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>It is the most prevalent type of dementia, accounting for 60-70% of cases. <sentence_start/>There are various hypotheses describing the possible pathophysiology of Alzheimer's disease (Fig. 1), of which the main ones are the amyloid beta (Aβ) and tau hypotheses (Fig. 1A and B), supported by the most extensive body of experimental and clinical data. <sentence_start/>In general, Alzheimer's disease is defined by the extracellular deposition of senile plaques, primarily composed of Aβ peptides, and the intracellular accumulation of neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs) formed by abnormally hyperphosphorylated tau protein,<citation rid="fcag332-B3" ref-type="bibr" pmid="33986301" doi="10.1038/s41572-021-00269-y" pmcid="PMC8574196" count="1"><sup>3</sup></citation> both of which are central to the process of neurodegeneration and cognitive decline.<citation rid="fcag332-B4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="27025652" doi="10.15252/emmm.201606210" pmcid="PMC4888851" count="1"><sup>4</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Tau protein is a microtubule-associated protein crucial for stabilizing neuronal microtubules and enabling axonal transport,<citation rid="fcag332-B5" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30507581" doi="10.3233/JAD-180868" count="1"><sup>5</sup></citation> while Aβ is a naturally occurring protein by-product that plays several physiological roles in the brain at lower, soluble levels, including antimicrobial protection, sealing blood-brain barrier leaks, promoting recovery from brain injury, supporting synapse formation and regulating long-term potentiation (memory consolidation) recently reviewed.<citation rid="fcag332-B6" ref-type="bibr" pmid="37239082" doi="10.3390/biomedicines11051411" pmcid="PMC10216198" count="1"><sup>6</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>More details on Alzheimer's disease pathophysiology mechanisms can be found in a recent review.<citation rid="fcag332-B2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39236855" doi="10.1016/j.arr.2024.102481" count="1"><sup>2</sup></citation>

<bold>The main hypotheses on the origin of Alzheimer’s disease and their underlying mechanisms (based on recent review</bold> <sup> <citation rid="fcag332-B2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39236855" doi="10.1016/j.arr.2024.102481" count="1">2</citation> </sup>): <bold>A</bold>) Aβ hypothesis: Alzheimer's disease is initiated by an imbalance between the production and clearance of amyloid beta (Aβ) peptides, particularly the aggregation-prone Aβ<sub>42</sub> isoform that arises from amyloid precursor protein (APP) processing via the amyloidogenic pathway, which involves β- and γ-secretases. <sentence_start/>These peptides aggregate into soluble oligomers and insoluble fibrils that deposit as plaques, disrupting synaptic function and triggering neuroinflammation. <sentence_start/>(<bold>B</bold>) The tau hypothesis: Abnormal hyperphosphorylation of the tau protein causes it to detach from microtubules and form aggregated neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs), the build-up of which leads to neuronal death. <sentence_start/>(<bold>C</bold>) Cholinergic hypothesis: Cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease is primarily due to a deficit in the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, resulting from the degeneration of cholinergic neurons. <sentence_start/>(<bold>D</bold>) Mitochondrial stress hypothesis: Mitochondrial dysfunction contributes to the formation of NFTs and senile plaques. <sentence_start/>This process is mediated by a cascade of cellular disturbances, including increased production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), increased oxidative stress, impaired energy metabolism and dysregulated calcium homeostasis. <sentence_start/>(<bold>E</bold>) Inflammation hypothesis: Prolonged activation of the brain's innate immune system, which primarily involves microglia and astrocytes, is a driver of Alzheimer's disease progression. <sentence_start/>The presence of aggregated Aβ in neural tissue promotes the activation of these glial cells, leading to increased production of proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β and IL-6) as well as ROS. <sentence_start/>(<bold>F</bold>) Neurovascular hypothesis: Impaired cerebral blood flow and the disruption of the neurovascular unit (NVU) lead to chronic hypoperfusion, which in turn reduces Aβ clearance, promotes oxidative stress and initiates inflammation. <sentence_start/>TNF, tumour necrosis factor; Based on the age of onset, Alzheimer's disease can be classified as early-onset Alzheimer's disease (EOAD, before age 65) or late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD, begins after age 65). <sentence_start/>Many metabolic and lifestyle factors are linked to Alzheimer's disease risk, but genetics contributes significantly to its complex pathophysiology, with the heritability estimates based on twin studies ranging from 60% to 80%, especially for LOAD.<sup><citation rid="fcag332-B7" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16461860" doi="10.1001/archpsyc.63.2.168" count="1">7</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B8" ref-type="bibr" pmid="35379992" doi="10.1038/s41588-022-01024-z" pmcid="PMC9005347" count="1">8</citation></sup> <sentence_start/>Lower values have been obtained in analyses of individual-level genome-wide association studies (GWAS) data from unrelated individuals (from 24% to 55%).<citation rid="fcag332-B9" ref-type="bibr" pmid="37131074" doi="10.1038/s41380-023-02076-1" pmcid="PMC10615767" count="1"><sup>9</sup></citation>

EOAD is often linked to familial Alzheimer's disease (fAD), an autosomal dominant form often caused by variants in or near the Aβ region of the <italic toggle="yes">APP</italic> gene,<citation rid="fcag332-B10" ref-type="bibr" pmid="25531812" doi="10.1001/jamaneurol.2014.2157" pmcid="PMC4324097" count="1"><sup>10</sup></citation> or <italic toggle="yes">PSEN1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">PSEN2</italic> variants, which alter γ-secretase function (Fig. 1A), increasing the production of aggregation-prone Aβ<sub>42</sub> and causing midlife Aβ deposition.<citation rid="fcag332-B4" ref-type="bibr" pmid="27025652" doi="10.15252/emmm.201606210" pmcid="PMC4888851" count="1"><sup>4</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>While all autosomal dominant fAD cases are EOAD, not all EOAD cases are familial; many are sporadic with unclear genetic and environmental causes;<citation rid="fcag332-B11" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21911656" doi="10.1001/archneurol.2011.221" pmcid="PMC3332307" count="1"><sup>11</sup></citation> therefore, only a minority (1-2%) of EOAD cases can be explained solely by known rare variants (in the <italic toggle="yes">APP</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PSEN1</italic>, or <italic toggle="yes">PSEN2</italic> gene); rather, most involve common genetic variants in other Alzheimer's disease associated genes.

LOAD is more common and often referred to as sporadic Alzheimer's disease, though familial clustering is observed in some cases. <sentence_start/>LOAD is influenced by complex genetic, environmental and lifestyle factors. <sentence_start/>Genetic contributors are mainly common but incompletely penetrant variants in numerous genes, such as those in the <italic toggle="yes">APOE</italic> gene.<citation rid="fcag332-B3" ref-type="bibr" pmid="33986301" doi="10.1038/s41572-021-00269-y" pmcid="PMC8574196" count="1"><sup>3</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Many of these variants have been discovered thanks to Alzheimer's disease genome-wide association studies (AD-GWAS) that rather than focusing on single candidate genes scan hundreds of thousands to millions of small nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in large populations to uncover loci linked to the disease. <sentence_start/>Thus, most cases of LOAD, but many EOAD cases as well, appear to be influenced by numerous genetic variants, each contributing a small effect. <sentence_start/>Consequently, Alzheimer's disease is often regarded as a complex polygenic disorder<citation rid="fcag332-B12" ref-type="bibr" pmid="37024668" doi="10.1038/s43856-023-00269-x" pmcid="PMC10079691" count="1"><sup>12</sup></citation> shaped by both genetics and the environment.

Data on genetic variants and their potential role in Alzheimer's disease pathophysiology is growing with the use of next-generation sequencing (NGS) technologies, especially whole-genome sequencing (WGS), which is used also in large-scale population studies and holds strong potential for widespread clinical adoption. <sentence_start/>In this review, we summarize the current understanding of the complex roles played by different types of genetic variants in Alzheimer's disease (Fig. 2). <sentence_start/>While early studies focused mainly on common single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), these explain only a fraction of the genetic risk. <sentence_start/>Therefore, we discuss not only small variants (including SNPs identified in AD-GWAS studies) but also larger-scale changes or structural variants (SVs) that can contribute to Alzheimer's disease risk<citation rid="fcag332-B13" ref-type="bibr" pmid="40528303" doi="10.1002/alz.70277" pmcid="PMC12173831" count="1"><sup>13</sup></citation> and possibly help to explain so-called ‘missing heritability’.<citation rid="fcag332-B14" ref-type="bibr" pmid="36907103" doi="10.1016/j.ebiom.2023.104511" pmcid="PMC10024184" count="1"><sup>14</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>These include copy number variations (CNVs), transposable elements (TEs)-related changes and tandem repeats (TRs). <sentence_start/>Selected examples of different variant types subdivided by the functional category of involved Alzheimer's disease genes are summarized in Supplementary Table 2. <sentence_start/>We also examine another critical layer of genetic complexity in Alzheimer's disease: somatic mosaicism in brain tissues, a phenomenon in which postzygotic <italic toggle="yes">de novo</italic> variants create genetically distinct cell populations within a single individual.<citation rid="fcag332-B15" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12360233" doi="10.1038/nrg906" count="1"><sup>15</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Moreover, we discuss the potential of polygenic risk score (PGS) and polygenic hazard score (PHS) calculations in Alzheimer's disease risk assessment, along with the integration of genomic data with other <italic toggle="yes">omics</italic> and AI-driven analyses to enhance biomarker discovery and individualized risk prediction. <sentence_start/>Thus, WGS enables new approaches that reveal layers of Alzheimer's disease heritability beyond traditional SNP/GWAS models and are reshaping the future of risk stratification.
Figure 2

<bold>Simplified representation and main characteristics of the different genetic variant types discussed in this review.</bold> <sentence_start/>Single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) represent the smallest genomic changes and can impact gene regulation or protein function. <sentence_start/>By definition, single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) are SNVs with a minor allele frequency of ≥1%. <sentence_start/>Additionally, small insertions and deletions (indels) may disrupt coding sequences or influence splicing and are readily identified by variant callers during point/small variants analysis from short-read WGS data. <sentence_start/>Copy number variations (CNVs) are larger structural variants that alter gene dosage (gain/loss) and have been linked to neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative conditions. <sentence_start/>Tandem repeats (TRs), including short tandem repeats (STRs) and variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs), usually influence gene expression and are implicated in repeat expansion disorders with neurological manifestations. <sentence_start/>Transposable elements (TEs), such as Alu, LINE-1 and SVA elements, can disrupt genes or regulatory regions through insertional mutagenesis and are increasingly recognized for their role in genome instability and somatic mosaicism in the ageing brain and Alzheimer’s disease. <sentence_start/>CNVs, TEs and TRs identification from short-read WGS or long-read sequencing data require dedicated tools, pipelines and databases that are discussed in the text (created by Google Slides).
Potential of WGS technologies for Alzheimer's disease research and risk stratification

While whole exome sequencing (WES) can be used to identify variants within the coding region of the major Alzheimer’s disease determining or influencing genes, here, we focus specifically on the use of WGS that provides the most comprehensive view of an individual's genetic makeup. <sentence_start/>Unlike more targeted methods, in a single analysis, WGS covers the entire genome, including both coding and non-coding regions, and enables the detection of a wider variety of genetic variants. <sentence_start/>This is particularly valuable for research and diagnosis of complex diseases, where the genetic cause(s) may reside outside of the protein-coding exome. <sentence_start/>Depending on read length and WGS strategy, WGS data can be generated using short-read (such as Illumina) and long-read platforms (such as PacBio HiFi, Oxford Nanopore (ONT)), with typical read length from 25 to 400 bp and from thousands to millions of bp, respectively.<citation rid="fcag332-B16" ref-type="bibr" pmid="34050336" doi="10.1038/s41576-021-00367-3" pmcid="PMC8161719" count="1"><sup>16</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Owing to its higher accuracy and throughput, short-read sequencing is widely used for detecting single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) and small indels; however, it has some limitations in reliably detecting variants in repetitive regions (including TR expansions) and larger SVs, which are usually better detected by long-reads. <sentence_start/>A more detailed overview of these technologies is provided in another review article.<citation rid="fcag332-B17" ref-type="bibr" pmid="38608738" doi="10.1016/j.ygeno.2024.110842" count="1"><sup>17</sup></citation>

Despite the still relatively high cost and the robust computational and data storage infrastructure needed for clinical application, the WGS offers significant opportunities, offering a single, comprehensive approach, replacing the need for multiple separate tests. <sentence_start/>It has already been reported as an effective tool for the diagnosis of neurological disorders because of its strong specificity and sensitivity,<citation rid="fcag332-B18" ref-type="bibr" pmid="35182509" doi="10.1016/S1474-4422(21)00462-2" pmcid="PMC8850201" count="1"><sup>18</sup></citation> indicating its clinical potential also for complex diseases. <sentence_start/>Once WGS becomes routine in healthcare, it is likely that this genetic information will become a standard component of many individuals’ medical records. <sentence_start/>With continually improving analytical tools and databases, WGS data can be reanalysed whenever necessary to obtain an updated view of a patient's condition and an improved understanding of disease risk or diagnosis. <sentence_start/>Within the specific context of Alzheimer’s disease, WGS has recently been used in the Alzheimer's disease sequencing project as a tool for better understanding the complexity and genetic background of the disease, aiming at detecting missing genetic factors influencing Alzheimer's disease.<citation rid="fcag332-B19" ref-type="bibr" pmid="40407102" doi="10.1002/alz.70237" pmcid="PMC12100500" count="1"><sup>19</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, full interpretation of WGS data requires integration with other <italic toggle="yes">omics</italic> layers, as discussed later in this review.
Rare and common small-scale variants in Alzheimer's disease

Small-scale DNA variants, such as SNVs (which refer to any single-nucleotide variant), SNPs (common SNVs with minor allele frequency ≥ 1%) as well as small indels play a key role in understanding the genetic architecture of Alzheimer's disease. <sentence_start/>These variants and their specific roles in the disease have recently been reviewed in more detail.<citation rid="fcag332-B20" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39885961" doi="10.1212/NXG.0000000000200224" pmcid="PMC11781270" count="1"><sup>20</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>They are mainly rare high-impact variants in genes like <italic toggle="yes">APP</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PSEN1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">PSEN2</italic> that can explain some fAD/EOAD cases (Table 1). <sentence_start/>It is important to emphasize that rare pathogenic variants in <italic toggle="yes">MAPT</italic> gene encoding tau protein are not among them, but <italic toggle="yes">MAPT</italic> variants are instead firmly established as the cause of ‘tauopathies’ (diseases characterized by tau tangles, like familial frontotemporal dementia (FTD)).<citation rid="fcag332-B5" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30507581" doi="10.3233/JAD-180868" count="1"><sup>5</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>However, certain common variants within <italic toggle="yes">MAPT</italic> have been identified as Alzheimer's disease risk modifiers (such as p.Ala152Thr), which are not fully penetrant and act by promoting tau protein aggregation.<citation rid="fcag332-B21" ref-type="bibr" pmid="22556362" doi="10.1093/hmg/dds161" pmcid="PMC3392107" count="1"><sup>21</sup></citation>

However, the majority of Alzheimer's disease cases are not monogenic. <sentence_start/>Most LOAD (but also EOAD) cases are influenced by common SNPs in many other genes that modulate its risk (Table 1). <sentence_start/>Many of them have been identified through GWAS studies,<citation rid="fcag332-B8" ref-type="bibr" pmid="35379992" doi="10.1038/s41588-022-01024-z" pmcid="PMC9005347" count="1"><sup>8</sup></citation> which have become a cornerstone of Alzheimer's disease research by enabling the systematic identification of common genetic variants associated with disease risk across the entire genome. <sentence_start/>Importantly, GWAS findings have shifted the understanding of Alzheimer's disease from a purely amyloid-centric disorder to a more complex, multifactorial condition. <sentence_start/>The major and best-established genetic risk locus for Alzheimer's disease is <italic toggle="yes">APOE</italic>. <sentence_start/>The three primary <italic toggle="yes">APOE</italic> isoforms ɛ4, ɛ3 and ɛ2 are determined by the specific combination of two SNPs (rs429358 and rs7412) located within the gene.<citation rid="fcag332-B22" ref-type="bibr" pmid="32818802" doi="10.1016/j.ebiom.2020.102954" pmcid="PMC7452404" count="1"><sup>22</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Of these, <italic toggle="yes">APOE</italic> ɛ4 (rs429358-C and rs7412-C) significantly increases the risk of LOAD, most likely through the impact on myelination.<citation rid="fcag332-B23" ref-type="bibr" pmid="36385529" doi="10.1038/s41586-022-05439-w" pmcid="PMC9870060" count="1"><sup>23</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The importance of this risk factor is underpinned by the fact that approximately 40% of patients diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease carry at least one copy of the <italic toggle="yes">APOE</italic> ɛ4.<citation rid="fcag332-B24" ref-type="bibr" pmid="9343467" count="1"><sup>24</sup></citation>

Thanks to the use of large biobanks for GWAS, the identification of other SNPs and genetic loci linked to Alzheimer's disease has recently accelerated and some new discoveries are still to be expected. <sentence_start/>In the past decade alone, the number of such loci has increased from 20 to over 118.<sup><citation rid="fcag332-B14" ref-type="bibr" pmid="36907103" doi="10.1016/j.ebiom.2023.104511" pmcid="PMC10024184" count="1">14</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/2025.10.10.25337470" count="1">25</citation></sup> <sentence_start/>For example, common (but also rare) risk-associated SNPs were identified in genes such as <italic toggle="yes">CLU</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">BIN1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PICALM</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">TREM2</italic> (Table 1), involved in pathways like amyloid processing, lipid metabolism, inflammation and synaptic function.<citation rid="fcag332-B26" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39612989" doi="10.1016/j.arr.2024.102599" count="1"><sup>26</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Individually, these SNPs usually confer modest effects, but together they contribute to a polygenic risk profile that influences susceptibility, age of onset and disease progression, making them valuable for research into mechanisms, risk prediction and potential therapeutic targets.<citation rid="fcag332-B8" ref-type="bibr" pmid="35379992" doi="10.1038/s41588-022-01024-z" pmcid="PMC9005347" count="1"><sup>8</sup></citation>
Rare variant burden

Interestingly, sequencing in fAD pedigrees negative for <italic toggle="yes">APP, PSEN1</italic> or <italic toggle="yes">PSEN2</italic> variants together with subsequent larger exome studies indicates that truncating or ultra-rare missense variants (with a dominant negative effect) in different domains of the SORL1 protein have a disease-causing effect in Alzheimer's disease.<sup><citation rid="fcag332-B27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13024-025-00907-z" pmcid="PMC12667055" pmid="41327266" count="1">27</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B28" ref-type="bibr" pmid="22472873" doi="10.1038/mp.2012.15" count="1">28</citation></sup> <sentence_start/>Therefore, further discoveries are still expected in this field, especially thanks to rare variant burden analyses that compare the prevalence of rare, potentially deleterious variants within a particular gene in individuals with Alzheimer's disease to unaffected controls. <sentence_start/>Since individual rare variants are typically observed in only a small number of individuals, analyses of single variants often lack sufficient statistical power. <sentence_start/>By aggregating multiple variants within a gene, such burden tests enhance the ability to identify gene-level associations that might otherwise remain undetected. <sentence_start/>Such variants have effect sizes larger than GWAS loci (moderate to large effect size), and it is believed they could elucidate part of the missing heritability in Alzheimer's disease. <sentence_start/>This approach gained significant traction especially following the discovery of rare variants in <italic toggle="yes">TREM2</italic><citation rid="fcag332-B29" ref-type="bibr" pmid="23150934" doi="10.1056/NEJMoa1211851" pmcid="PMC3631573" count="1"><sup>29</sup></citation> and loss-of-function variants in <italic toggle="yes">ABCA7.</italic><citation rid="fcag332-B30" ref-type="bibr" pmid="25807283" doi="10.1038/ng.3246" count="1"><sup>30</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>So far, at least 13 genes have been reported that either increase or decrease the Alzheimer’s disease risk through such rare genetic variants, and other promising candidate genes with a rare variant burden signal have been identified.<citation rid="fcag332-B31" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39905212" doi="10.1038/s41582-025-01062-1" count="1"><sup>31</sup></citation>
Small-scale DNA variant genotyping and interpretation

Genotyping SNVs and small indels depends on the data type, scale and accuracy needs. <sentence_start/>Identification of rare high-impact variants linked to EOAD/fAD (in genes <italic toggle="yes">APP</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PSEN1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">PSEN2,</italic> Table 1) and evaluation of their pathogenicity follow the same rules as for monogenic diseases (American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) criteria<citation rid="fcag332-B32" ref-type="bibr" pmid="25741868" doi="10.1038/gim.2015.30" pmcid="PMC4544753" count="1"><sup>32</sup></citation>), using databases such as gnomAD,<sup><citation rid="fcag332-B33" ref-type="bibr" pmid="32461654" doi="10.1038/s41586-020-2308-7" pmcid="PMC7334197" count="1">33</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.64898/2026.03.23.26349081" count="1">34</citation></sup> ClinVar,<citation rid="fcag332-B35" ref-type="bibr" pmid="29165669" doi="10.1093/nar/gkx1153" pmcid="PMC5753237" count="1"><sup>35</sup></citation> and OMIM<citation rid="fcag332-B36" ref-type="bibr" pmid="25428349" doi="10.1093/nar/gku1205" pmcid="PMC4383985" count="1"><sup>36</sup></citation> can aid interpretation.

GWASs have traditionally relied on DNA arrays to analyse known SNPs via hybridization, but this method misses novel variants. <sentence_start/>New solutions have been developed to extend coverage, such as SNP imputation (uses reference panels such as the 1000 Genomes Project) and more recent GWASs already use WGS technology to analyse SNPs genome-wide. <sentence_start/>GWAS typically identifies variants with small effect sizes, usually requiring very large sample sizes, and translating these associations into biological mechanisms remains a major ongoing challenge. <sentence_start/>Bias towards European ancestry may be reduced by including more individuals from different populations.<citation rid="fcag332-B37" ref-type="bibr" pmid="41087731" doi="10.1038/s41431-025-01951-5" pmcid="PMC12669238" count="1"><sup>37</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Details on GWAS methodology can be found in a recent review.<citation rid="fcag332-B38" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>38</sup></citation>

Genotyping arrays followed by genotype imputation can also be used to increase genomic coverage in general and improve power for locus discovery. <sentence_start/>This approach has enabled the identification of numerous Alzheimer's disease risk loci, including genes involved in amyloid processing, lipid metabolism and immune pathways. <sentence_start/>However, the advantage of WGS approach is that it provides simultaneous genotyping (for GWAS) and identification of possible rare ‘determining’ variants.<citation rid="fcag332-B39" ref-type="bibr" pmid="32519380" doi="10.1002/gepi.22326" pmcid="PMC7449570" count="1"><sup>39</sup></citation>

Based on the sequencing technology and laboratory, several tools can be used that employ statistical or machine learning (ML) models to distinguish true variants from erroneous calls, which are typically caused by low coverage, mapping ambiguity or other technical biases. <sentence_start/>To test genetic associations of identified SNPs with continuous or binary traits/phenotypes, linear or logistic regression models are used, respectively, applying a Bonferroni significance threshold (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic> < 5 × 10<sup>−8</sup>) to reduce false positives. <sentence_start/>Common approaches for rare variant burden testing include Combined Multivariate and Collapsing (CMC),<citation rid="fcag332-B40" ref-type="bibr" pmid="18691683" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2008.06.024" pmcid="PMC2842185" count="1"><sup>40</sup></citation> Sequence Kernel Association Test (SKAT)<citation rid="fcag332-B41" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21737059" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2011.05.029" pmcid="PMC3135811" count="1"><sup>41</sup></citation> and SKAT-O.<citation rid="fcag332-B42" ref-type="bibr" pmid="22863193" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2012.06.007" pmcid="PMC3415556" count="1"><sup>42</sup></citation>
Copy number variation variants (CNVs)

CNVs are deletions or duplications of genomic segments (typically ranging from kilobases to megabases) that alter gene dosage and contribute substantially to human genetic diversity and disease susceptibility.<citation rid="fcag332-B43" ref-type="bibr" pmid="34649833" doi="10.1016/j.bj.2021.02.003" pmcid="PMC8640565" count="1"><sup>43</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>In Alzheimer’s disease, CNVs represent an important class of structural variation because they can affect both canonical Alzheimer’s disease genes and broader pathways related to immunity, lipid metabolism, synaptic function and neuronal resilience.
Biological relevance of CNVs in Alzheimer's disease

Among the best-established CNVs in Alzheimer's disease is <italic toggle="yes">APP</italic> duplication, which causes autosomal dominant EOAD by increasing amyloid precursor protein (APP) dosage and accelerating Aβ accumulation.<citation rid="fcag332-B44" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16369530" doi="10.1038/ng1718" count="1"><sup>44</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Deletions affecting <italic toggle="yes">PSEN1</italic> exon 9 have likewise been linked to rare fAD cases.<citation rid="fcag332-B45" ref-type="bibr" pmid="9546792" doi="10.1038/nm0498-452" count="1"><sup>45</sup></citation>

Beyond these canonical loci, CNVs in immune-related genes such as <italic toggle="yes">CR1</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">CHRFAM7A</italic> have also been implicated in Alzheimer’s disease risk. <sentence_start/>Duplication of the low-copy repeat within the <italic toggle="yes">CR1</italic> locus has been associated with increased risk, likely through altered complement activity,<sup><citation rid="fcag332-B46" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21403675" doi="10.1038/mp.2011.24" pmcid="PMC3265835" count="1">46</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B47" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19734903" doi="10.1038/ng.439" count="1">47</citation></sup> whereas variation involving <italic toggle="yes">CHRFAM7A</italic> may affect α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor signalling.<sup><citation rid="fcag332-B46" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21403675" doi="10.1038/mp.2011.24" pmcid="PMC3265835" count="1">46</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B48" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21660214" doi="10.4061/2011/729478" pmcid="PMC3109875" count="1">48</citation></sup>

Recent exome-wide analyses have highlighted additional rare CNVs in Alzheimer’s disease, including events affecting genes such as <italic toggle="yes">MAPT</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">ABCA1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">ABCA7</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">TYROBP</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">CTSB</italic>, as well as recurrent CNVs in regions such as 22q11.21.<citation rid="fcag332-B49" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2026.07.013" pmid="42648288" count="1"><sup>49</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Other reported CNVs involve loci linked to synaptic and neurodevelopmental function, detoxification (<italic toggle="yes">SULT1A3/4</italic>) and carbohydrate metabolism (<italic toggle="yes">AMY1A</italic>),<citation rid="fcag332-B50" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28374858" doi="10.1038/tpj.2017.4" count="1"><sup>50-53</sup></citation> with additional network-based analyses suggesting broader effects on pathways related to inflammation, signalling and disease progression.<citation rid="fcag332-B54" ref-type="bibr" pmid="38020759" doi="10.3389/fnagi.2023.1241412" pmcid="PMC10652415" count="1"><sup>54</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Together, these findings suggest that CNVs may influence Alzheimer’s disease susceptibility, age of onset and clinical heterogeneity through dosage effects across multiple disease-relevant pathways. <sentence_start/>Selected CNVs associated with Alzheimer’s disease, including recurrent pathogenic events, candidate loci and variants linked to clinical heterogeneity, are summarized in Supplementary Table 1.

One important mechanism by which CNVs may contribute to Alzheimer’s disease is altered gene expression. <sentence_start/>Integrative genomic and transcriptomic studies have shown that CNVs can modulate genes involved in memory, immunity and vascular function, including <italic toggle="yes">CREB1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">FAM119A</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">HLA-DRA</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">TLR1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PLAU</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">PLGRKT.</italic><sup><citation rid="fcag332-B55" ref-type="bibr" pmid="23168992" doi="10.1038/tp.2012.119" pmcid="PMC3565761" count="1">55</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B56" ref-type="bibr" pmid="22486522" doi="10.2174/156720512802455331" pmcid="PMC3500615" count="1">56</citation></sup> <sentence_start/>An example is an 8-kb deletion upstream of <italic toggle="yes">CREB1</italic>, which increases Alzheimer’s disease risk by disrupting regulation within a linked chromosomal region.<citation rid="fcag332-B55" ref-type="bibr" pmid="23168992" doi="10.1038/tp.2012.119" pmcid="PMC3565761" count="1"><sup>55</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>CNVs may also influence chromatin organization and transcriptional regulation in neurons.<citation rid="fcag332-B57" ref-type="bibr" pmid="36846102" doi="10.3389/fnagi.2022.1073905" pmcid="PMC9944073" count="1"><sup>57</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>These effects may be relevant not only for disease risk, but also for phenotype modulation, including psychosis, progression-related traits and other aspects of clinical variability in Alzheimer’s disease.<sup><citation rid="fcag332-B51" ref-type="bibr" pmid="34918867" doi="10.1002/alz.12507" pmcid="PMC9264340" count="1">51</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B54" ref-type="bibr" pmid="38020759" doi="10.3389/fnagi.2023.1241412" pmcid="PMC10652415" count="1">54</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B58" ref-type="bibr" pmid="26035058" doi="10.1038/tp.2015.64" pmcid="PMC4490277" count="1">58</citation></sup>
Detection of CNVs in the NGS era

CNV analysis from an NGS perspective remains challenging because CNVs must be inferred indirectly from sequencing signals such as read depth, read-pair orientation, split reads and local assembly, which often generate large and noisy callsets.<citation rid="fcag332-B59" ref-type="bibr" pmid="38340093" doi="10.1093/bib/bbae022" pmcid="PMC10858679" count="1"><sup>59</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>This is consistent with large Alzheimer’s disease WGS studies, in which CNV or SV detection relied on multiple callers and subsequent harmonization or joint genotyping before downstream analysis.<sup><citation rid="fcag332-B51" ref-type="bibr" pmid="34918867" doi="10.1002/alz.12507" pmcid="PMC9264340" count="1">51</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B52" ref-type="bibr" pmid="34804120" doi="10.3389/fgene.2021.752390" pmcid="PMC8599981" count="1">52</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B60" ref-type="bibr" pmid="40038788" doi="10.1186/s13073-025-01444-6" pmcid="PMC11881306" count="1">60</citation></sup> <sentence_start/>Short-read WGS generally performs well for larger CNVs and genome-wide dosage profiling, but it is less reliable in repetitive regions and often provides limited breakpoint resolution for complex events. <sentence_start/>Long-read sequencing can overcome part of these limitations by improving breakpoint definition, resolving repetitive or structurally complex loci and facilitating phasing, although its current use in Alzheimer’s disease remains more limited because of cost, throughput and analytical demands.<citation rid="fcag332-B61" ref-type="bibr" pmid="38510277" doi="10.3389/fgene.2024.1374860" pmcid="PMC10951082" count="1"><sup>61</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>WGS can improve resolution of rare or complex CNVs compared with array-based approaches, but robust analysis still requires stringent filtering and validation.<sup><citation rid="fcag332-B51" ref-type="bibr" pmid="34918867" doi="10.1002/alz.12507" pmcid="PMC9264340" count="1">51</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B52" ref-type="bibr" pmid="34804120" doi="10.3389/fgene.2021.752390" pmcid="PMC8599981" count="1">52</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B60" ref-type="bibr" pmid="40038788" doi="10.1186/s13073-025-01444-6" pmcid="PMC11881306" count="1">60</citation></sup> <sentence_start/>CNVs are then typically interpreted by annotating gene content, overlap with known Alzheimer’s disease loci and predicted dosage sensitivity, followed by integration with diagnosis, age at onset, Braak and CERAD scores for quantifying neuropathological features of Alzheimer’s disease, biomarker profiles and transcriptomic data.<sup><citation rid="fcag332-B51" ref-type="bibr" pmid="34918867" doi="10.1002/alz.12507" pmcid="PMC9264340" count="1">51</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B52" ref-type="bibr" pmid="34804120" doi="10.3389/fgene.2021.752390" pmcid="PMC8599981" count="1">52</citation></sup> <sentence_start/>Large Alzheimer’s disease multi-omics studies have further used CNV-gene-trait correlation networks to link CNVs with gene-expression changes and disease-relevant pathways.<citation rid="fcag332-B51" ref-type="bibr" pmid="34918867" doi="10.1002/alz.12507" pmcid="PMC9264340" count="1"><sup>51</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>For germline CNVs, ACMG/ClinGen-based frameworks and tools such as ClassifyCNV can support classification.<citation rid="fcag332-B62" ref-type="bibr" pmid="33230148" doi="10.1038/s41598-020-76425-3" pmcid="PMC7683568" count="1"><sup>62</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>For somatic or single-cell CNVs, interpretation requires particularly stringent filtering, denoising, and orthogonal validation because low-frequency events are highly susceptible to technical artefacts.<citation rid="fcag332-B63" ref-type="bibr" pmid="36451207" doi="10.1186/s40478-022-01452-2" pmcid="PMC9714068" count="1"><sup>63</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>This caution is also supported by single-cell studies in Alzheimer’s disease neurons showing that conclusions depend strongly on post-calling filtering and noise reduction.<citation rid="fcag332-B63" ref-type="bibr" pmid="36451207" doi="10.1186/s40478-022-01452-2" pmcid="PMC9714068" count="1"><sup>63</sup></citation>
Transposable element-related variants (TEs)

TEs, including long interspersed nuclear elements (LINEs), short interspersed nuclear elements (SINEs), LTR retrotransposons and DNA transposons, comprise a substantial fraction of the human genome.<citation rid="fcag332-B64" ref-type="bibr" pmid="22144907" doi="10.1371/journal.pgen.1002384" pmcid="PMC3228813" count="1"><sup>64</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Although most are epigenetically silenced, a subset remains active and can promote genomic instability through insertions, deletions and rearrangements.<citation rid="fcag332-B65" ref-type="bibr" pmid="35269693" doi="10.3390/ijms23052551" pmcid="PMC8910135" count="1"><sup>65</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>In Alzheimer’s disease, TEs are increasingly considered a potential source of both genomic and regulatory variation.
TE-related variants and their relevance in Alzheimer’s disease

Among human TEs, SINE-VNTR-Alu (SVA) elements are a hominid-specific class of non-autonomous retrotransposons that may contribute to Alzheimer's disease-relevant repeat variation.<citation rid="fcag332-B66" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39875385" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-56400-0" pmcid="PMC11775329" count="1"><sup>66</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>In Alzheimer's disease-associated loci, structural variation within SVA elements, including variants near <italic toggle="yes">BIN1</italic>, has been linked to gene-regulatory effects, and STR expansions enriched within SVA retrotransposons have also been reported in Alzheimer’s disease.<sup><citation rid="fcag332-B66" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39875385" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-56400-0" pmcid="PMC11775329" count="1">66</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B67" ref-type="bibr" pmid="35332097" doi="10.1101/gr.275515.121" pmcid="PMC8997352" count="1">67</citation></sup> <sentence_start/>Alu insertions within <italic toggle="yes">TOMM40</italic> intron 6, a region in strong linkage disequilibrium with <italic toggle="yes">APOE</italic>, have also been proposed to contribute to Alzheimer's disease-related genetic variation.<citation rid="fcag332-B68" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28242298" doi="10.1016/j.jalz.2017.01.017" pmcid="PMC6647845" count="1"><sup>68</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The poly-T repeat rs10524523 co-segregates with <italic toggle="yes">APOE</italic> isoforms, with longer alleles associated with <italic toggle="yes">APOE</italic> ɛ4 and shorter variants with ɛ2/ɛ3.<citation rid="fcag332-B68" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28242298" doi="10.1016/j.jalz.2017.01.017" pmcid="PMC6647845" count="1"><sup>68</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>An Alu-associated structural variant in the <italic toggle="yes">TMEM106B</italic> 3′UTR has also been linked to dementia-related traits, further supporting the view that TE-derived non-coding variation may modify disease-relevant phenotypes beyond canonical Alzheimer’s disease risk loci.<citation rid="fcag332-B60" ref-type="bibr" pmid="40038788" doi="10.1186/s13073-025-01444-6" pmcid="PMC11881306" count="1"><sup>60</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Collectively, these observations suggest that TE-derived variants may modulate Alzheimer’s disease susceptibility through both regulatory effects and linkage with established risk loci.

TEs may also contribute to disease through transcriptional dysregulation. <sentence_start/>A TE expression quantitative trait loci analysis identified more than 26 000 TE loci associated with gene expression in aged Alzheimer’s disease brains, including a SINE element linked to repression of <italic toggle="yes">C1QTNF4.</italic><citation rid="fcag332-B69" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39356058" doi="10.1002/alz.14164" pmcid="PMC11567813" count="1"><sup>69</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Tau pathology has likewise been associated with activation of retrotransposons, including LINE-1 and endogenous retroviruses, in post-mortem human brains and experimental models.<citation rid="fcag332-B70" ref-type="bibr" pmid="29874575" doi="10.1016/j.celrep.2018.05.004" pmcid="PMC6181645" count="1"><sup>70</sup></citation>
Detection of TE-variants in the NGS era

TEs represent one of the most technically challenging classes of variants to analyse using NGS, owing to their repetitive sequence content and frequent occurrence in structurally complex loci. <sentence_start/>Such sequences are poorly resolved by standard short-read approaches, which may miss insertions, misclassify breakpoints, or yield ambiguous alignments. <sentence_start/>Long-read platforms such as PacBio and ONT improve the detection of full-length insertions and structurally complex TE loci. <sentence_start/>However, reliable analysis still depends on specialized bioinformatic workflows, stringent filtering and careful downstream interpretation, particularly when linking TE-derived calls to Alzheimer's disease-relevant genes or regulatory mechanisms.<sup><citation rid="fcag332-B71" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39558574" doi="10.1093/bioinformatics/btae686" pmcid="PMC11601167" count="1">71</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B72" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39414821" doi="10.1038/s41467-024-53294-2" pmcid="PMC11484939" count="1">72</citation></sup>
Tandem repeat variants (TRs) in Alzheimer’s disease

TRs, comprising 3-6% of the genome and found at more than 2 million loci, may represent another key source of genetic variation in Alzheimer’s disease.<citation rid="fcag332-B73" ref-type="bibr" pmid="34140671" doi="10.1038/s41580-021-00382-6" pmcid="PMC9612635" count="1"><sup>73</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>TRs generally vary by motif size and structure: short tandem repeats (STRs) (2-6 bp) and VNTRs (≥7 bp), with some VNTRs spanning full genes.<citation rid="fcag332-B74" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31659027" doi="10.1073/pnas.1912175116" pmcid="PMC6859368" count="1"><sup>74</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>While not all TRs are variable, if they have multiple alleles, they potentially exert greater functional effects than do biallelic SNPs. <sentence_start/>Owing to their high degree of polymorphism and instability, STRs are implicated in more than 40 monogenic neurodegenerative disorders, in which disease severity often correlates with expansion size (for review see<citation rid="fcag332-B75" ref-type="bibr" pmid="33811808" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2021.03.011" pmcid="PMC8205997" count="1"><sup>75</sup></citation>). <sentence_start/>TR changes can cause disease through mechanisms depending on the repeat location, sequence composition and gene context. <sentence_start/>Many known diseases causing STRs lie within exons, introns, or UTRs, but their impact on protein functions goes beyond direct coding roles (reviewed recently<citation rid="fcag332-B73" ref-type="bibr" pmid="34140671" doi="10.1038/s41580-021-00382-6" pmcid="PMC9612635" count="1"><sup>73</sup></citation>), and many are known to colocalize with enhancers or transcription start sites, affecting gene regulation.<citation rid="fcag332-B76" ref-type="bibr" pmid="26642241" doi="10.1038/ng.3461" pmcid="PMC4909355" count="1"><sup>76</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The majority of STRs, however, are intergenic, and their changes can modulate gene expression or chromatin organization, often in a tissue-specific manner.<citation rid="fcag332-B77" ref-type="bibr" pmid="32522982" doi="10.1038/s41467-020-16482-4" pmcid="PMC7286898" count="1"><sup>77</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Recent studies have also linked an increased burden of STR expansions to polygenic disorders such as autism and schizophrenia,<citation rid="fcag332-B78" ref-type="bibr" pmid="33442040" doi="10.1038/s41586-020-03078-7" pmcid="PMC7810352" count="1"><sup>78-80</sup></citation> confirming a potential role for TRs in Alzheimer’s disease risk.
TRs loci associated with Alzheimer’s disease

Several studies have examined the relationship between VNTRs and LOAD, mostly focussing on specific VNTRs of interest, such as those in the <italic toggle="yes">ABCA7</italic><citation rid="fcag332-B81" ref-type="bibr" pmid="37946268" doi="10.1186/s13195-023-01338-y" pmcid="PMC10634183" count="1"><sup>81</sup></citation> and <italic toggle="yes">INS</italic><citation rid="fcag332-B82" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12111440" doi="10.1007/s007020200086" count="1"><sup>82</sup></citation> genes, and another one near <italic toggle="yes">MUC6,</italic><citation rid="fcag332-B83" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31748784" doi="10.1093/jnen/nlz116" pmcid="PMC8204704" count="1"><sup>83</sup></citation> or STR in the 5'UTR of the <italic toggle="yes">RELN</italic><citation rid="fcag332-B84" ref-type="bibr" pmid="18599960" doi="10.3233/jad-2008-14308" count="1"><sup>84</sup></citation> gene (Supplementary Table 1). <sentence_start/>More recently, genome-wide analyses have extended these findings. <sentence_start/>A VNTR-based study in 9501 individuals from the Alzheimer’s disease Sequencing Project identified nine novel VNTRs associated with Alzheimer’s disease diagnosis, cognitive decline and brain imaging traits, several of which colocalized with known expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) or Alzheimer’s disease risk loci.<citation rid="fcag332-B85" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39980902" doi="10.1212/NXG.0000000000200241" pmcid="PMC11839231" count="1"><sup>85</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>In parallel, a large STR association study in approximately 330 000 UK Biobank participants, including clinically diagnosed and proxy Alzheimer’s disease cases, reported 14 independent STR loci associated with Alzheimer’s disease risk.<citation rid="fcag332-B86" ref-type="bibr" pmid="42243151" doi="10.1038/s41467-026-73902-7" pmcid="PMC13237113" count="1"><sup>86</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Most overlapped known SNP-based GWAS regions, but additional STR signals were reported near <italic toggle="yes">SNX32</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">WBS1.</italic><citation rid="fcag332-B86" ref-type="bibr" pmid="42243151" doi="10.1038/s41467-026-73902-7" pmcid="PMC13237113" count="1"><sup>86</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Interestingly, the <italic toggle="yes">SNX32</italic> gene, which is involved in neuronal differentiation in neuroglial cells in vitro,<citation rid="fcag332-B87" ref-type="bibr" pmid="37158588" doi="10.7554/eLife.84396" pmcid="PMC10219652" count="1"><sup>87</sup></citation> was recently highlighted in a proteome-wide association study to be causally involved in Alzheimer’s disease pathogenesis.<citation rid="fcag332-B88" ref-type="bibr" pmid="33510477" doi="10.1038/s41588-020-00773-z" pmcid="PMC8130821" count="1"><sup>88</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>In addition, several other loci have been delineated, in which STRs (and not SNPs) represent the lead association signal (ABCA7) or make substantial contributions to SNP-driven GWAS associations (HLA-DRB1, MINDY/ADAM10 and APOE).<citation rid="fcag332-B86" ref-type="bibr" pmid="42243151" doi="10.1038/s41467-026-73902-7" pmcid="PMC13237113" count="1"><sup>86</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The same study also estimated that STRs explain at least 3% of Alzheimer's disease phenotypic variance. <sentence_start/>Aligning the top STRs with DNA methylation and transcriptome profiles from human brain samples suggests that several STRs may affect gene expression.
Increased burden of STR expansions in Alzheimer’s disease

Another genome-wide analysis of PCR-free WGS data from 2981 individuals with and without disease showed that Alzheimer’s disease cases carry a greater burden of rare and longer STR expansions across the genome.<citation rid="fcag332-B66" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39875385" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-56400-0" pmcid="PMC11775329" count="1"><sup>66</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Most polymorphic STRs were located in intronic (47.4%) or distal noncoding regions (36.7%), whereas only a small fraction occurred in promoters (14.1%) or coding exons (0.76%).<citation rid="fcag332-B66" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39875385" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-56400-0" pmcid="PMC11775329" count="1"><sup>66</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Statistical analysis revealed that if >30 STR expansions were found, the person was 3.69-fold more likely to have Alzheimer’s disease and also to have more severe neuropathology. <sentence_start/>Study findings support a polygenic burden model in which the cumulative effect of multiple STR expansions, rather than a single repeat locus, contributes to disease risk, similar to models proposed for autism and schizophrenia.<citation rid="fcag332-B78" ref-type="bibr" pmid="33442040" doi="10.1038/s41586-020-03078-7" pmcid="PMC7810352" count="1"><sup>78-80</sup></citation>

There were 6276 and 5229 unique STR expansions observed in Alzheimer’s disease individuals (AD-STR expansions) and controls, respectively,<citation rid="fcag332-B66" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39875385" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-56400-0" pmcid="PMC11775329" count="1"><sup>66</sup></citation> with 213 STR expansions present in 5 or more Alzheimer’s disease individuals. <sentence_start/>AD-STR expansions were slightly but significantly longer, 50.1% of them were dinucleotide repeats, whereas only 2.1% had a repeat unit of 6 bp or longer.<citation rid="fcag332-B66" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39875385" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-56400-0" pmcid="PMC11775329" count="1"><sup>66</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>It was demonstrated that although most AD-STR expansions were not protein coding, they were highly enriched near genes implicated in biological processes with known relevance to Alzheimer’s disease pathophysiology, such as ‘neuron projection morphogenesis’ and ‘axon development’.<citation rid="fcag332-B66" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39875385" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-56400-0" pmcid="PMC11775329" count="1"><sup>66</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>When AD-STR expansions present within genes (exons, untranslated regions or introns) were examined, enrichment in gene sets related to synaptic function was observed. <sentence_start/>For example, in the <italic toggle="yes">GRID2</italic> gene they identified 7 STR expansions across 9 individuals with Alzheimer’s disease (only 1 STR in 1 control individual). <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">GRID2</italic> encodes a subunit of the glutamate receptor and has a recognized role in synaptic transmission.<citation rid="fcag332-B89" ref-type="bibr" pmid="7736576" doi="10.1016/0092-8674(95)90334-8" count="1"><sup>89</sup></citation>
Broader genomic instability in Alzheimer’s disease

The widespread distribution of STR expansions across the genome raises the possibility that Alzheimer’s disease is associated with broader genomic instability rather than variation at only a few repeat loci.<citation rid="fcag332-B66" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39875385" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-56400-0" pmcid="PMC11775329" count="1"><sup>66</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Interestingly, prior findings indicate that individuals with Alzheimer’s disease also have a greater burden of rare coding SNVs<citation rid="fcag332-B90" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30820047" doi="10.1038/s41588-019-0358-2" pmcid="PMC6463297" count="1"><sup>90</sup></citation> and SVs.<citation rid="fcag332-B13" ref-type="bibr" pmid="40528303" doi="10.1002/alz.70277" pmcid="PMC12173831" count="1"><sup>13</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Two non-exclusive models have been proposed: either ageing and Alzheimer’s disease-related pathology promote repeat instability, or unstable inherited and/or somatic TR alleles contribute to disease pathogenesis.<citation rid="fcag332-B66" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39875385" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-56400-0" pmcid="PMC11775329" count="1"><sup>66</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Together, these findings suggest that TRs represent an underappreciated layer of Alzheimer’s disease-related genetic variation, acting through both locus-specific and genome-wide effects.
Challenges of TR detection and genotyping

TR detection remains technically challenging because repetitive regions are difficult to genotype accurately from standard sequencing data. <sentence_start/>With short-read WGS, many TRs exceed the read length (∼150 bp), leading to partial alignments, stutter noise and imprecise sizing of large alleles.<citation rid="fcag332-B91" ref-type="bibr" pmid="38366034" doi="10.1038/s41576-024-00692-3" count="1"><sup>91</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Reliable analysis therefore depends on sequencing depth, careful quality control (QC) and dedicated tools for genotyping and expansion discovery. <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, there are tools such as GangSTR<citation rid="fcag332-B92" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31194863" doi="10.1093/nar/gkz501" pmcid="PMC6735967" count="1"><sup>92</sup></citation> or ExpansionHunterDenovo,<citation rid="fcag332-B93" ref-type="bibr" pmid="32345345" doi="10.1186/s13059-020-02017-z" pmcid="PMC7187524" count="1"><sup>93</sup></citation> which enable genome-wide STR genotyping in large cohorts, allowing Alzheimer’s disease association studies. <sentence_start/>Long-read platforms can improve accuracy by sequencing full TRs and flanking regions in single reads, resolving complex structures,<citation rid="fcag332-B94" ref-type="bibr" pmid="38965568" doi="10.1186/s13059-024-03319-2" pmcid="PMC11229021" count="1"><sup>94</sup></citation> though they are less accessible so far. <sentence_start/>Importantly, short-read approaches remain effective: a recent study<citation rid="fcag332-B66" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39875385" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-56400-0" pmcid="PMC11775329" count="1"><sup>66</sup></citation> found strong concordance with PacBio data.

Because TR definitions and reference catalogues differ across tools, no single method captures the full spectrum of repeat variation. <sentence_start/>Efforts towards consensus callsets and large TR catalogues are ongoing, but many remain biased towards European populations. <sentence_start/>The TR-Atlas,<citation rid="fcag332-B95" ref-type="bibr" pmid="38582080" doi="10.1016/j.cell.2024.03.004" pmcid="PMC11065452" count="1"><sup>95</sup></citation> currently the most comprehensive reference, profiles ∼860 000 TRs from 338 963 WGS samples (39.5% non-European). <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, broader inclusion of diverse populations is still needed to reduce ancestry bias and improve assessment of TR variation across populations.
Somatic mosaicism in Alzheimer’s disease

Somatic mosaicism, defined as genetically distinct cell populations arising from postzygotic mutations, has emerged as a potential contributor to the complexity of Alzheimer’s disease pathogenesis. <sentence_start/>It is particularly relevant in the brain, where postmitotic neurons accumulate DNA alterations over time.<citation rid="fcag332-B96" ref-type="bibr" pmid="36266706" doi="10.1186/s13039-022-00624-y" pmcid="PMC9585840" count="1"><sup>96</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>In addition to sporadic SNVs, mosaic SVs, CNVs and aneuploidies have been reported in post-mortem Alzheimer’s disease brains.<citation rid="fcag332-B96" ref-type="bibr" pmid="36266706" doi="10.1186/s13039-022-00624-y" pmcid="PMC9585840" count="1"><sup>96</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Because these events are often low-frequency, region-specific and cell-type restricted, they are difficult to detect and interpret using standard NGS approaches.<citation rid="fcag332-B97" ref-type="bibr" pmid="37716438" doi="10.1016/j.mrrev.2023.108471" pmcid="PMC10843083" count="1"><sup>97</sup></citation>
Biological and clinical relevance of somatic mosaicism in Alzheimer's disease

Brain-specific mosaic SNVs have been identified in Alzheimer’s disease genes, including <italic toggle="yes">PSEN1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">PSEN2</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">APP</italic>,<citation rid="fcag332-B98" ref-type="bibr" pmid="25937274" doi="10.1016/j.jalz.2015.02.007" count="1"><sup>98</sup></citation> and, as well as in additional loci with potential functional relevance in neuronal survival or Alzheimer’s disease-related pathways.<sup><citation rid="fcag332-B99" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31216356" doi="10.1093/hmg/ddz085" pmcid="PMC6688063" count="1">99</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B100" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31300647" doi="10.1038/s41467-019-11000-7" pmcid="PMC6626023" count="1">100</citation></sup> <sentence_start/>Mosaic CNVs, particularly <italic toggle="yes">APP</italic> copy-number gains, may increase gene dosage and promote amyloid pathology.<citation rid="fcag332-B101" ref-type="bibr" pmid="25650802" doi="10.7554/eLife.05116" pmcid="PMC4337608" count="1"><sup>101</sup></citation> <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">APP</italic>-associated mosaic events may also influence phenotype: mosaic <italic toggle="yes">APP</italic> triplication was associated with later disease onset than constitutional triplication,<citation rid="fcag332-B102" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39849058" doi="10.1038/s41598-025-86645-0" pmcid="PMC11759332" count="1"><sup>102</sup></citation> suggesting that mutation burden and distribution may modify disease severity. <sentence_start/>Somatic <italic toggle="yes">APP</italic> gene recombination has also been proposed to generate neuronal genomic cDNAs, although this interpretation remains controversial.<citation rid="fcag332-B103" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30464338" doi="10.1038/s41586-018-0718-6" pmcid="PMC6391999" count="1"><sup>103</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>More broadly, recurrent chromosomal abnormalities, including mosaic chromosome 21 alternations and X chromosome loss, provide additional evidence for somatic mosaicism in Alzheimer’s disease brains.<citation rid="fcag332-B104" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24602248" doi="10.1186/1755-8166-7-20" pmcid="PMC3995993" count="1"><sup>104</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>However, its precise pathogenic contribution remains unresolved. <sentence_start/>Together, these findings suggest that somatic mosaic variation may contribute to both biological and clinical heterogeneity in Alzheimer’s disease beyond germline mutations.
Detection of somatic mosaicism in the NGS era

From an NGS perspective, somatic mosaicism is challenging because true variants must be distinguished from sequencing artefacts, especially at very low variant allele frequencies.<citation rid="fcag332-B97" ref-type="bibr" pmid="37716438" doi="10.1016/j.mrrev.2023.108471" pmcid="PMC10843083" count="1"><sup>97</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Deep sequencing has identified somatic SNVs in post-mortem Alzheimer’s disease hippocampus,<citation rid="fcag332-B100" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31300647" doi="10.1038/s41467-019-11000-7" pmcid="PMC6626023" count="1"><sup>100</sup></citation> while high-depth single-cell WGS has shown increased somatic mutational burden in Alzheimer’s disease neurons.<citation rid="fcag332-B105" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/2022.04.21.489103" count="1"><sup>105</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Tools such as Mutect2,<citation rid="fcag332-B106" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/861054" count="1"><sup>106</sup></citation> Strelka2,<citation rid="fcag332-B107" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30013048" doi="10.1038/s41592-018-0051-x" count="1"><sup>107</sup></citation> and SCcaller<citation rid="fcag332-B108" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28319112" doi="10.1038/nmeth.4227" pmcid="PMC5408311" count="1"><sup>108</sup></citation> support the analysis of ultra-deep and single-cell data, but robust detection still requires stringent filtering, orthogonal validation and careful downstream interpretation.<sup><citation rid="fcag332-B97" ref-type="bibr" pmid="37716438" doi="10.1016/j.mrrev.2023.108471" pmcid="PMC10843083" count="1">97</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B98" ref-type="bibr" pmid="25937274" doi="10.1016/j.jalz.2015.02.007" count="1">98</citation></sup>

Integration of genomic and single-cell transcriptomic data enables cell-type-aware analysis of somatic variation by linking mosaic variants to specific neuronal and glial populations and by revealing their potential transcriptional consequences.<sup><citation rid="fcag332-B51" ref-type="bibr" pmid="34918867" doi="10.1002/alz.12507" pmcid="PMC9264340" count="1">51</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B52" ref-type="bibr" pmid="34804120" doi="10.3389/fgene.2021.752390" pmcid="PMC8599981" count="1">52</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B105" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/2022.04.21.489103" count="1">105</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B109" ref-type="bibr" pmid="37123987" doi="10.1212/NXG.0000000000200066" pmcid="PMC10136684" count="1">109</citation></sup> <sentence_start/>Such approaches can help distinguish broadly distributed mutations from lineage-restricted or cell-type-specific events, thereby improving interpretation of the functional relevance of somatic variation in Alzheimer’s disease brain tissue.<sup><citation rid="fcag332-B105" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/2022.04.21.489103" count="1">105</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B109" ref-type="bibr" pmid="37123987" doi="10.1212/NXG.0000000000200066" pmcid="PMC10136684" count="1">109</citation></sup> <sentence_start/>Duplex sequencing further improves the detection of ultra-low-frequency variants by suppressing sequencing artefacts and increasing confidence in rare variant calls.<sup><citation rid="fcag332-B97" ref-type="bibr" pmid="37716438" doi="10.1016/j.mrrev.2023.108471" pmcid="PMC10843083" count="1">97</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B110" ref-type="bibr" pmid="33911282" doi="10.1038/s41586-021-03477-4" count="1">110</citation></sup> <sentence_start/>In parallel, emerging long-read approaches may improve resolution of somatic structural variation, repeat-rich regions and complex breakpoints that are difficult to resolve with short-read data alone.<sup><citation rid="fcag332-B97" ref-type="bibr" pmid="37716438" doi="10.1016/j.mrrev.2023.108471" pmcid="PMC10843083" count="1">97</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B110" ref-type="bibr" pmid="33911282" doi="10.1038/s41586-021-03477-4" count="1">110</citation></sup> <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, these strategies remain constrained by tissue quality, uneven cellular representation, sequencing depth, cost and the need for specialized analytical workflows and orthogonal validation. <sentence_start/>Overall, NGS-based and single-cell approaches have substantially expanded the study of somatic mosaicism in Alzheimer’s disease, but major technical and interpretative challenges remain.
Polygenic risk score (PGS) and polygenic hazard score (PHS) in Alzheimer's disease research

PGS serves to estimate an individual’s lifetime genetic susceptibility to complex polygenic traits or diseases. <sentence_start/>While PGS estimates an individual’s lifetime genetic predisposition to a disease as a static measure (typically interpreted as a relative risk), PHS incorporates time-to-event (survival) modelling, estimating age-specific risk, thereby providing a dynamic prediction of when the disease is likely to occur rather than just whether it will occur. <sentence_start/>In Alzheimer’s disease research, PGS and PHS can be used to stratify individuals by genetic risk and support the identification of risk factors, thereby contributing to earlier detection and improved understanding of disease mechanisms.<citation rid="fcag332-B111" ref-type="bibr" pmid="35848019" doi="10.3233/JAD-220025" pmcid="PMC9484091" count="1"><sup>111</sup></citation>
PGS and PHS calculation methods and data sources

The schematic PGS workflow is illustrated in Fig. 3A. <sentence_start/>In general, PGS calculation is based on GWAS-identified SNP datasets that have been shown to be significantly associated with a complex trait, taking into account the effect of these SNPs on the development of a given complex trait in general.<citation rid="fcag332-B112" ref-type="bibr" pmid="32709988" doi="10.1038/s41596-020-0353-1" pmcid="PMC7612115" count="1"><sup>112</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>One of the key sources of GWAS data is the NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog.<citation rid="fcag332-B115" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39530240" doi="10.1093/nar/gkae1070" pmcid="PMC11701593" count="1"><sup>115</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>While GWAS focus primarily on common SNPs, currently, emerging studies also explore CNVs, although integration into standard GWAS frameworks remains limited.<citation rid="fcag332-B116" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39375560" doi="10.1038/s41576-024-00778-y" pmcid="PMC12329314" count="1"><sup>116</sup></citation>
Figure 3

<bold>General workflow for calculating polygenic risk score (PGS) from genomic data and the main factors influencing its accuracy.</bold> <sentence_start/>(<bold>A</bold>) Workflow of PGS: To perform PGS calculations, base and target data are necessary. <sentence_start/>The base data include SNPs associated with a complex trait, each carrying an effect size measured by beta (β) for continuous traits or odds ratios (ORs), specifically logOR, for binary traits. <sentence_start/>These SNPs are typically identified through GWAS and are provided as summary statistics, with a genome-wide significance threshold of <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> < 5 × 10<sup>−8</sup>.<citation rid="fcag332-B112" ref-type="bibr" pmid="32709988" doi="10.1038/s41596-020-0353-1" pmcid="PMC7612115" count="1"><sup>112</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The target data consisted of genotype (list of annotated SNPs) and phenotype (clinical) information from the tested individuals. <sentence_start/>(<bold>B)</bold> Factors affecting PGS accuracy: A cohort size of ≥100 individuals is recommended.<citation rid="fcag332-B112" ref-type="bibr" pmid="32709988" doi="10.1038/s41596-020-0353-1" pmcid="PMC7612115" count="1"><sup>112</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>There is limited transferability of PGS across non-European ancestries, which stems from insufficient diversity in GWASs.<citation rid="fcag332-B113" ref-type="bibr" pmid="37620596" doi="10.1038/s41576-023-00637-2" pmcid="PMC10961971" count="1"><sup>113</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Inaccuracies in effect allele assignment, genome build mismatches, poor ancestry matching, or unresolved ambiguous, duplicate, or mismatching SNPs between base and target data can all contribute to reduced accuracy and introduce systematic bias in the analysis.<sup><citation rid="fcag332-B112" ref-type="bibr" pmid="32709988" doi="10.1038/s41596-020-0353-1" pmcid="PMC7612115" count="1">112</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B114" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31999256" doi="10.7554/eLife.48376" pmcid="PMC7067566" count="1">114</citation></sup> rs, reference SNP cluster identifier (also called rsID) for SNP variants (created in BioRender. <sentence_start/>Pös, O. (2026) ).

The simplest approach to calculate PGS<citation rid="fcag332-B117" ref-type="bibr" pmid="18250146" doi="10.1373/clinchem.2007.095489" count="1"><sup>117</sup></citation> for an individual is to sum the number of associated alleles (0, 1, or 2) across all associated SNPs, each weighted by its respective effect size. <sentence_start/>It is possible that multiple SNPs associated with Alzheimer’s disease risk are in linkage disequilibrium (LD), effectively tagging the same underlying risk region. <sentence_start/>To avoid double-counting this shared genetic signal, thus improving predictive accuracy of the PGS,<citation rid="fcag332-B118" ref-type="bibr" pmid="26430803" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2015.09.001" pmcid="PMC4596916" count="1"><sup>118</sup></citation> commonly used PGS methods apply LD-based clumping and thresholding (C + T), which selects a set of approximately independent variants by excluding those in high LD. <sentence_start/>Alternatively, newer methods retain all SNPs and use an LD matrix with Bayesian priors (statistical approaches) to shrink and reweight SNP effects in high-LD regions (e.g. LDpred2, PRS-CS, SBayesR), improving genetic risk estimation.<citation rid="fcag332-B118" ref-type="bibr" pmid="26430803" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2015.09.001" pmcid="PMC4596916" count="1"><sup>118</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>PGS accuracy depends on several factors (Fig. 3B), and QC is crucial for base and target data in order to meet high-quality standards. <sentence_start/>A valuable source of systematically evaluated and openly accessible PGS scoring files together with standardized metadata required for their reproducible application is the PGS Catalog.<citation rid="fcag332-B119" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>119</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>It enables researchers to directly apply previously published PGS models to their own genotype data without the need to reconstruct scores from original GWAS summary statistics, thereby facilitating benchmarking, cross-cohort comparisons and independent validation of genetic risk models.<citation rid="fcag332-B120" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39327485" doi="10.1038/s41588-024-01937-x" pmcid="PMC12041910" count="1"><sup>120</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>The PGS Catalog follows FAIR principles (findability, accessibility, interoperability and reusability) and enables automated PGS calculation via the PGS Catalog calculator (pgsc_calc),<citation rid="fcag332-B120" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39327485" doi="10.1038/s41588-024-01937-x" pmcid="PMC12041910" count="1"><sup>120</sup></citation> while PgsRankRnnotatR tool can be used to prioritize Alzheimer’s disease-related PGS datasets from curated sources (such as PGS Catalog).<citation rid="fcag332-B121" ref-type="bibr" pmid="39967687" doi="10.3389/fgene.2025.1507395" pmcid="PMC11832703" count="1"><sup>121</sup></citation>

Unlike PGS, PHS is established on slightly adjusted standard case-control GWAS summary statistics. <sentence_start/>PHS incorporates time-to-event (survival) modelling, estimating age-specific risk. <sentence_start/>For this purpose, Cox Proportional Hazard Regression (Cox regression) analysis is utilized,<citation rid="fcag332-B122" ref-type="bibr" count="1"><sup>122</sup></citation> to estimate the hazard ratio (HR), a measure between the probability of events in a ‘case’ group compared to the probability of events in a ‘control’ group. <sentence_start/>Therefore, PHS uses log(HR) as SNP risk allele weights, instead of β used for continuous traits or odds ratios (ORs), specifically ln(OR), for binary traits in PGS (Fig. 3).<citation rid="fcag332-B123" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28323831" doi="10.1371/journal.pmed.1002258" pmcid="PMC5360219" count="1"><sup>123</sup></citation>
Use of PGS in Alzheimer’s disease risk estimation

The current stage of Alzheimer's disease PGS (AD-PGS) research focuses not only on testing the influence of SNPs in the <italic toggle="yes">APOE</italic> ɛ4 isoform<sup><citation rid="fcag332-B124" ref-type="bibr" pmid="33532541" doi="10.1002/dad2.12142" pmcid="PMC7821873" count="1">124</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B125" ref-type="bibr" pmid="34386572" doi="10.1002/dad2.12226" pmcid="PMC8339682" count="1">125</citation></sup> but also on evaluating the influence of SNPs in other associated genes (e.g. <italic toggle="yes">APP</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">GFAP</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">NFL</italic>)<citation rid="fcag332-B126" ref-type="bibr" pmid="35001095" doi="10.1038/s41386-021-01258-1" pmcid="PMC8938514" count="1"><sup>126-128</sup></citation> and the impact of all common SNPs on changes in PGS distribution.<sup><citation rid="fcag332-B129" ref-type="bibr" pmid="34099642" doi="10.1038/s41467-021-22491-8" pmcid="PMC8184987" count="1">129</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B130" ref-type="bibr" pmid="32226939" doi="10.1093/braincomms/fcz047" pmcid="PMC7100005" count="1">130</citation></sup> <sentence_start/>In general, the development of AD-PGS aims to improve the prediction of early risk and the stratification of individuals on the basis of their genetic susceptibility. <sentence_start/>Therefore, some PGS studies examined the distributions of EOAD and LOAD,<citation rid="fcag332-B131" ref-type="bibr" pmid="32968074" doi="10.1038/s41467-020-18534-1" pmcid="PMC7511365" count="1"><sup>131</sup></citation> the link between genetic risk and biomarkers,<sup><citation rid="fcag332-B126" ref-type="bibr" pmid="35001095" doi="10.1038/s41386-021-01258-1" pmcid="PMC8938514" count="1">126</citation>,<citation rid="fcag332-B132" ref-type="bibr" pmid="35383826" doi="10.1093/brain/awac128" pmcid="PMC9924904" count="1">132</citation></sup> and the influence of non-genetic factors on dementia-related PGS calculations.<citation rid="fcag332-B133" ref-type="bibr" pmid="30181149" doi="10.1503/cmaj.180066" pmcid="PMC6148649" count="1"><sup>133</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>However, according to Bellenguez <italic toggle="yes">et al</italic>.,<citation rid="fcag332-B8" ref-type="bibr" pmid="35379992" doi="10.1038/s41588-022-01024-z" pmcid="PMC9005347" count="1"><sup>8</sup></citation> the developed AD-PGS has shown limited predictive power beyond standard risk factors such as age, sex and <italic toggle="yes">APOE</italic> ɛ4 isoform, as well as poor transferability to non-European populations. <sentence_start/>Substantially increasing the GWAS sample size might help to overcome these limitations and also reveal otherwise hidden common variants, helping to provide a finite set of SNP variants that are significant for Alzheimer's disease risk determination.<citation rid="fcag332-B134" ref-type="bibr" pmid="36224396" doi="10.1038/s41586-022-05275-y" pmcid="PMC9605867" count="1"><sup>134</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>This might also help to clarify whether the condition follows a polygenic or oligogenic genetic architecture.<citation rid="fcag332-B131" ref-type="bibr" pmid="32968074" doi="10.1038/s41467-020-18534-1" pmcid="PMC7511365" count="1"><sup>131</sup></citation>

Moreover, different approaches have to be investigated, since some pathogenic processes associated with the disease may be driven by genetic variants that are not necessarily among those defined directly as the ‘susceptibility to Alzheimer’s disease’ identified by GWAS. <sentence_start/>For example, GWAS sets based on the levels of different cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers (i.e. Aβ and tau protein) have led to identification of independent genetic variants also involved in Alzheimer’s disease susceptibility.<citation rid="fcag332-B135" ref-type="bibr" pmid="36066633" doi="10.1007/s00401-022-02454-z" pmcid="PMC9547780" count="1"><sup>135</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>Similarly, a GWAS focused on cognitive performance in over 300 000 individuals identified loci overlapping with Alzheimer’s disease risk regions,<citation rid="fcag332-B136" ref-type="bibr" pmid="29844566" doi="10.1038/s41467-018-04362-x" pmcid="PMC5974083" count="1"><sup>136</sup></citation> indicating that GWASs capture only part of the genetic variance in Alzheimer’s disease, thus, a PGS derived from GWAS summary statistics alone may not fully capture the total genetic risk in an Alzheimer’s disease patient.

From a methodological point of view, also various PGS calculation approaches have been used for Alzheimer’s disease risk estimation, including C + T (PRSice) and Bayesian approaches (DBSLMM, LDpred2, PRS-CS and SBayesR).<citation rid="fcag332-B111" ref-type="bibr" pmid="35848019" doi="10.3233/JAD-220025" pmcid="PMC9484091" count="1"><sup>111</sup></citation>

Traditional AD-PGS methods, which estimate disease risk by summing all the identified phenotype-relevant risk alleles, weighted by their effect size, can be effective in ascertaining the overall risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease. <sentence_start/>Instead, pathway-specific PGS (only variants in genes affecting specific molecular pathways associated with Alzheimer's disease are used) can be better at predicting specific biomarkers of pathology, such as Aβ deposition.<citation rid="fcag332-B137" ref-type="bibr" pmid="34521561" doi="10.1016/j.neurobiolaging.2021.08.005" count="1"><sup>137-139</sup></citation> <sentence_start/>A pathway-specific approach can also help to identify the pathways affected to a greater extent in some individuals than in others, eventually enabling a more personalized approach to potential therapy selection in the future.
